title: Watch and pray (Luke 21:29–38)
hook: don't let your hearts be weighed down with cares; watch and pray

segments.voice: Yesterday, apolytrosis: when the world shakes, lift up your heads. Your line was your redemption draws near.

Jesus has been saying hard things about the end: wars, signs, Jerusalem surrounded by armies. His closing words aren't about armies at all. They're about a fig tree in leaf, and the weight a person carries all day and takes to bed at night. The unanswered email. The bill. The thing a sister said at dinner. Eleven at night, the day is over, and the mind is still running. His warning reads as if it were written for that hour.

First the tree. When the fig tree and all the trees put out leaves, you know summer is near. Nobody needs a calendar; you just look. Then a sentence about what lasts: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." And the warning, in the King James words: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares." Overcharged: the Greek means weighed down, made heavy. Three things on the list. Surfeiting: the Greek word is used for the heavy head after a night of drinking, something close to a hangover. Drunkenness. And cares of this life: ordinary worries. He puts worry on the same list as a hangover; both leave the heart too heavy to notice what's coming. Then the cure: "Watch ye therefore, and pray always." The Greek for watch means to stay awake, like a guard on night duty. Not anxious. Alert. Luke ends the chapter with Jesus living it out. By day he teaches in the temple. Every night he goes out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. Early every morning, the people come to hear him. Not a slogan for a crisis, but a rhythm: carry the day lightly enough that you can still see the leaves.
screen: then, large: `WATCH YE THEREFORE, AND PRAY ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Notice what's sitting heaviest on you today and name it plainly, in a few words. Imagine it as an actual weight in your hands, and without solving anything, set it down for tonight on the floor beside the bed; it will still be there in the morning if you need it. If you pray, hand it to God by name.
Surfeiting, the heavy, hungover feeling Jesus warns can weigh a heart down, along with drunkenness and ordinary cares.
Your line: carry the day lightly enough. The fig tree is already in leaf. That's day five hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some Christians keep an evening prayer, such as Compline, to hand over the day before sleep, and some churches read this chapter in the season of Advent.

fork.setup: Jesus has warned of hard days ahead. what does he say is most likely to make people miss the day when it comes?
options: not studying the signs closely enough.
hearts weighed down with excess and the cares of this life.
fork.reveal: "lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life." ordinary heaviness, not a lack of information.

original.note: Greek: stay awake, keep from sleeping. the word Luke uses for 'watch' in 21:36.

trapdoor: what you thought: be on high alert for the end of the world.
what it means: don't let excess or worry make your heart so heavy you can't see what's coming; stay awake and keep praying.
what a scholar hears: 'overcharged' renders a Greek verb for weighing down, and 'watch' is agrypneo, to go without sleep, the language of a sentry.
recall: a speck of faith that could move a tree
guess: the heavy head after too much drink
a sudden flood that drowns the fields
too much sleep, a lazy kind of rest

chat.says: Jesus warned about drunkenness. Why does he put everyday worries on the same list?
options: Both weigh the heart down, so you're too heavy to notice what's coming.
Because worry makes people drink, so he's really only warning about drinking.
He didn't; worry isn't on the list, only overeating and drinking.
chat.meaning: Surfeiting, drunkenness and cares of this life all overcharge the heart, weighing it down, so the day comes unawares. The cure: watch and pray.

surfeiting.meaning: the heavy head after drinking, close to a hangover

cares of this life.meaning: ordinary worries, on the list with drunkenness

Mount of Olives.meaning: where Jesus spent each night that week

sources.quoted: Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.
Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
Watch ye therefore, and pray always

notes: 'Overcharged' renders a form of the Greek bareo, to weigh down; 'watch' renders agrypneo, to be sleepless. Confirm.
Luke 21:37 says he 'abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives'; the script says he went out to spend the night there; the Greek verb can mean to lodge in the open. Confirm.
Original-language form ἀγρυπνεῖτε (present imperative plural) as in Luke 21:36. Confirm accent and form.
